title: Canadian cost pressure, social connection, and care exit form a linked but non-causal consumer-social pressure pattern
source_unit: Mental Health Research Canada, Understanding the Mental Health of Canadians Poll 29: Economic pressures, social connections and care
geography: Canada; national online survey of people aged 16 and older

observations.period: July 27-August 10, 2026; national cost and household-pressure indicators

denominator.unit: online survey respondents aged 16+ in Canada; national results weighted by gender, age, and region

cost_of_living_negative_mental_health.unit: percent saying cost of living negatively affects their mental health

difficulty_paying_household_bills.unit: percent reporting difficulty fully paying household bills

difficulty_affording_stable_housing.unit: percent reporting difficulty affording or maintaining stable housing

global_political_events_pressure.unit: percent citing global political events as affecting mental health

climate_change_pressure.unit: percent citing climate change as affecting mental health

mechanism.value: Material and geopolitical pressure is entering the consumer-social field as perceived mental-health strain, but the survey does not establish a causal route from prices or uncertainty to mental health

observations.method: Online national population poll conducted by Pollara Strategic Insights for Mental Health Research Canada; results weighted using recent census data for gender, age, and region; reported margin of error ±1.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.
observations.uncertainty: This is a sponsor-led cross-sectional online survey, not administrative hardship or clinical data. The measures are self-reported perceptions and cannot establish clinical diagnosis, actual arrears, housing loss, or causal effects.
observations.subgroup: People aged 16 and older in Canada, with weighted national estimates and selected higher-need subgroup analyses.
observations.counterinterpretation: Respondents may interpret cost, bills, housing, and mental-health impact differently; common causes such as employment, health, debt, household composition, or local prices may generate the correlations.

observations.period: July 27-August 10, 2026; social contact, coping, and connection barriers

denominator.unit: online survey respondents aged 16+ in Canada; national results weighted by gender, age, and region

weekly_family_meaningful_interaction.unit: percent reporting meaningful interactions with family at least weekly

weekly_friend_meaningful_interaction.unit: percent reporting meaningful interactions with friends at least weekly

weekly_neighbour_meaningful_interaction.unit: percent reporting meaningful interactions with neighbours at least weekly

weekly_community_group_meaningful_intera.unit: percent reporting meaningful interactions with community or organized groups at least weekly

connection_barrier_lack_of_time.unit: percent among people with fewer social connections identifying lack of time as a barrier

connection_barrier_mental_health.unit: percent among people with fewer social connections identifying mental-health challenges as a barrier

self_reliance_coping.unit: percent saying they keep busy or push through on their own when dealing with stress

distance_coping.unit: percent saying they take time alone or distance themselves from others when dealing with stress

mechanism.value: Connection is strongest in family and friend channels and thinner in neighbourhood and organized-group channels; time scarcity and self-reliance can constrain conversion from household strain into collective support

observations.method: Descriptive extraction from the weighted national Poll 29 online survey; connection questions and coping questions use the survey’s reported national or conditional denominators.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not observe contact duration, network quality, geographic isolation, cultural participation, or longitudinal change. Conditional percentages apply only to the relevant subgroup and cannot be compared as general-population prevalence.
observations.subgroup: Canadian adults and the conditional subgroup reporting fewer social connections.
observations.counterinterpretation: More family or friend contact may not mean more support; solitude can be chosen or protective; associations between connection and happiness or mental health may run in both directions.

observations.period: July 27-August 10, 2026; mental-health and substance-use support experience

denominator.unit: online survey respondents aged 16+ in Canada; care measures use conditional subgroups who accessed support

support_met_most_or_all_needs_past_year.unit: percent among people who accessed mental-health support in the past year saying support met most or all needs

support_fully_met_needs_past_year.unit: percent among people who accessed mental-health support in the past year saying needs were fully met

ended_care_early_past_five_years.unit: percent among people who accessed mental-health or substance-use support in the past five years saying they ended care earlier than planned or needed

severe_anxiety_fully_met.unit: percent among people with severe anxiety symptoms saying care fully met needs

severe_anxiety_early_exit.unit: percent among people with severe anxiety symptoms reporting early care exit

depression_fully_met.unit: percent among people with moderately severe to severe depression symptoms saying care fully met needs

depression_early_exit.unit: percent among people with moderately severe to severe depression symptoms reporting early care exit

mechanism.value: Access to care and realized continuity are separate stages: entering support does not imply full need satisfaction or continued engagement, especially among higher-need respondents

observations.method: Conditional subgroup estimates from the Poll 29 weighted online survey; the report identifies early-exit reasons including lack of real-world progress, not feeling understood or respected, and unclear goals or expectations.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reported retrospective care experiences, not verified clinical records or outcomes. Conditional denominators differ across support access, symptom severity, and early-exit measures; the survey cannot establish provider causality or treatment effectiveness.
observations.subgroup: Canadian respondents who accessed mental-health or substance-use support, including higher-symptom subgroups.
observations.counterinterpretation: Ending care early may reflect improvement, cost, scheduling, preference, provider mismatch, access barriers, or survey interpretation; unmet need and service failure should not be treated as identical.

boundary: This record adds a Canadian material-pressure, social-connection, and care-continuity layer. It does not establish clinical prevalence, causal effects of cost or connection, verified household hardship, cultural participation, or treatment quality.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official MHRC Poll 29 page reviewed for cost, housing, bills, social contact, coping, care satisfaction, early exit, symptom-severity subgroup, sample, weighting, sponsor, and non-causal statements.
